A group of men seated on the ground in the shade of a tree. Second from left is an elder, identified as Ubang-wi-Nyidoor, a nobleman who had his 'court' at Pinythin on the Akobo river. He was the acknowledged leader of the Ulueth lineage and as such had power over a number of villages in eastern Anuakland.

The huts of Dibango village seen from a distance over a stretch of dry cracked earth. Around the village is a derelict stockade of branches stuck in the ground, and in front of that a shallow ditch or moat, erected in the past as a form of defence against raids.

Hut roofs of the village of Ugak seen from a distance across a open area of fields. Predominantly agriculturalists, the Anuak clear the fields (often in forest soil) sometime around March and April and sow in May as the rains come on. Since Evans-Pritchard was in Anuakland during this part of the year only it is likely that this field has just been cleared of vegetation ready for sowing.

An expedition porter pulling a bullet from his cartridge belt, a rifle on the ground next to him. It was usual on such long expedition marches to shoot game to feed the group of carriers as well as to present to local people as gifts.

A view across a compound with huts and small children in Ukaadi village, towards a small fence plastered with mud and decorated with waving lines ornamented on the top with a fringe of grass tufts. The base of the courtyard fence is also decorated in a similar manner. It is probable that the small decorated fence was to the prevent occupants within the courtyard from being visible through the adjacent entrance way.

A group of youths seated on the ground around a nobleman (identified as Cam-war-Akwei) who is sitting on an antelope skin, wrapped in a textile with a European hat. This Cam-war-Akwei was one of three so-named sons of Akwei-wa-Cam, one of the most powerful nobles of the preceeding generation who lived at Utalo, and was head of a noble lineage. His brother, also called Cam, held the royal emblems from 1921-27 but died in colonial captivity in 1933.

An iron knife with a broad roughly sickle shaped blade and a wooden haft. At the base of the blade is a circular perforation through which a strip of leather has been tied and connects to the handle. Trumbash. A throwing knife with several limbs that are all pointed and double edged. With a leather bound handle secured with string.
Ndu kuna. Gourd with bulbous body and swelling at base of neck. Lengths of bark fibre knotted around waist. Used for carrying beer and water.

Circular wooden stool with central, spheroid support decorated with deeply incised wedges and circular foot. Seat is decorated around the perimeter with incised lines in triangular sections and a triangular cut-out close to one edge. Slightly chipped on foot and seat.
Woven hat with square top. Panel of dark brown decoration around the rim with geometric design in natural grass colour. Holes in each of the corners. Rim unravelling.
Women emptying dampened malted eleusine to germinate on the ground, covering them with further banana leaves to protect them from the sun, ready for the next stage of beer (gbangara) preparation.

A man and two women spreading out banana leaves for dampened malted eleusine to germinate on. They will then be covered in further banana leaves to protect them from the sun, ready for the next stage of beer (gbangara) preparation.

Two widows (dekurugbo) in the foreground (with shaven heads, one with string around torso) being ritually anointed with oil at the termination of their mourning period, when a feast is held. After a husband's death widows would have been expected to marry either his brother or another close male relative (levirate).

A small grass medicine shelter set within a garden. Since medicines to protect crops (such as bagbuduma) are vulnerable to damp and cold they were frequently placed in such shelters to protect them, or covered by an inverted pot or in the hollow of a tree.

Two men building up the clay inner wall of the common hut type known as gbuguru or gbasendeyo, which has long overhanging eaves creating a shaded area. This image shows how the walls are made, with relatively thin strips built up in layers by hand.

A portrait of a woman (identified as na Namarusu, i.e. the mother of Namarusu) standing at the entrance to her hut. The eaves above the door are propped up with a pole, supporting some baskets stored above the eaves.
Harpe arquée en ivoire et peau
Gbina kuli. Knotted plant fibre net tied to a length of unshaped stick and several unfired clay weights. For rats.
Moña; coin hair ornament. Three centime-pieces worn as hair ornaments.

Kumbu buda. Globular pot with neck divided in two and rejoined at the mouth; everted rim. Each neck is decorated with a moulded human face. The upper part of the body is decorated with curving lines of tiny semicircular impressions. The area below the mouth is decorated all over with semicircular impressions. Possibly used to contain oil.

Carved wooden male figure. Figure features a rounded hairstyle, vertical scarification marks on the cheeks, one arm curved downward, and one arm curved upward. Small white beads are attached as eyes; the genital area has been darkened; figure tilts slightly to one side.

Ire ga agangassi or mat used in boys' circumcision ceremonies. Rectangular mat woven from two colours of reed; design of two rows of concentric diamonds; twill plaiting with a double border and the ends bent over to form a fringe; red powdery pigment on one side of the mat, possibly ochre.

Iwa. Rubbing board oracle, used for divination. Consists of two wooden pieces tied together with a thin fibre rope. One piece of wood is circular with a cylindrical top protrusion; the other is circular with two legs and a roughly oval side protrusion. Used by rubbing the upper piece against the lower piece after a question is asked of the oracle; an answer is dependent on whether the upper piece sticks or slides off the lower piece.

Small lidded globular basket (.1), coiled construction with small decorative protrusions on sides and lid. A drinking cup made from a coconut shell with an ornate geometric design of bands and circles carved into the outside. It has a long, cylindrical wooden handle with carved decoration, that goes through a hole in the side of the cup. Pyrography has been used to decorate these carved sections.

A chief's drinking cup, carved from wood, with a rounded base, everted rim, and looped handle. The outside of the cup has been darkened using a flame, and there is an incised line with triangular sections carved around the middle.

A woman with a child on her lap wearing tukakao or chikobwela (wound copper or iron wire earrings), a string of beads interposed with stones and ornaments poses with an incelwa (bubble pipe) made from a kankuli (a gourd).
A man wearing a protective helmet holding a quant pole, Lake Kariba.
A woman with scarified arms and wearing tusambo (bracelets) bears two cisuo (baskets) on her head.

A musical bow, with gourd resonator and a metal wire string. The bow is made from wood and curves in at both ends. The string, likely made from brass or another copper alloy, is tied onto the bow at both ends. The resonator is made from half of a dark orange/brown gourd, and is attached to the bow with metal wire.
Simple wooden bow with tapered ends. Twisted hide string tied in tension to both ends of the shaft. The string is made from two parts tied together in the middle.

A vignette head-and-shoulders profile portrait of a Baka woman with lip ornaments and 'barbed harpoon' style cicatrices on her shoulder. Buchta made an excursion to the groups west of the Nile in 1879 setting out from Juba on 7th July and returning there on 26th August.

An upper body full face portrait of a seated Baka girl wearing a leaf pubic covering. She seems to have been photographed against a sheet marked with metric measurements (visible to the right) for recording height. This is the only photograph in the collection which shows this anthropometric measurement, but suggests that some of the other images may have originally have been taken to also provide such 'scientific' data. Portrait of a Mandara woman with her arms crossed over her chest, wearing a plant fibre skirt with a band of red and yellow beadwork. The woman has an upper lip piercing with a large circular white disc, as well as a nose and ear piercings. She is wearing a hide head band and metal bracelets on both wrists, and a variety of necklaces and girdles of multicoloured beadwork. Two small glass bottles with red caps hang at her chest.

Side portrait of a Mandara woman with facial scarifications and tattoos. Two seated Mandara women (referred to as Peanut Farmers) and a child gathered around a small fire, the child is eating peanuts. Mosaroze Moramenwa (also known as Rra Kesego) ploughing with donkeys in the molapo (seasonal flood plain) at Gweghiri, west of Shorobe. The grandson with white shoes is Boitlhoko Kgalalo, the one leading the donkeys is Lekgoana. In years past, these fields would have been watered with seasonal flood waters from the Okavango delta, but the gradual lessening of flood waters reaching the area had meant that farmers were relying on seasonal rains only.

Mosaroze Moramenwa (also known as Rra Kesego) with his crop of maize in the molapo (seasonal flood plain) at Gweghiri, west of Shorobe. Women in traditional tšale (shawl) and tuka (headscarf) at the wedding celebrations of Mosaroze Moramenwa in the newly made lolwapa of his daughter Kesego Kgalalo in Wenela ward, Maun. Mosaroze Moramenwa with his new wife, at the home of his daughter Kesego Kgalalo in Wenela ward, Maun. Kesego was the mother of Boitlhoko, Morton's fieldwork assistant. A store hut in the molapo area around Totoga near Shorobe village, unusually using stalks of maize crop for walling material. The owner was elderly, without money to buy letlhaka (water reeds, Phragmites australis) from the central Okavango swamp area.

Large group standing in village clearing, and in the foreground is a group of two men and four women who appear to be wearing high status or ceremonial dress. The men are wearing rectangular chest ornaments with rows of cowrie shells alternating with short goat hair fringes and long goat hair fringes round the edges, with a neck strap with cowrie shells and a long goat hair fringe. The men are also wearing bead necklaces with several strands. One of the men is wearing a black kilt with three rows of cowrie shells, and has a thick ivory armlet on each arm, indicating high status. Both men are wearing smaller brass armlets and beaded ear ornaments. One of the women is wearing a dark body cloth with white stripes, a bead necklace with several strands and large brass rings in her ears. The other three women, all of whom have shaven hair, are wearing white body cloths with black and white stripes, bead necklaces and large brass earrings which they have flipped upwards.  Behind the group is an elevated stone platform, and on it are four large baskets with conical lids and a fabric sack with carrying strap and a folded cane chair bound with straps. Behind the platform is a stone terrace, on which most of the group is standing. Individuals in the group are holding containers such as a folded leaf, a small basket, pottery vessel and a bamboo water vessel.

A tall cone-shaped hut with small entrance at base, probably in the homestead of the rain-making family of Tarangole, the main Lotuko village. The largest such huts were said to be some thirty feet high, with palm-leaf thatch touching the ground, an interior of some twenty feet across that included a subdivision by a low wall. The Seligmans visited Lotuko country in the early part of 1922, and according to their diary they travelled between these villages by bicycle.

Group photograph of a white man stood with two Datooga women 20 miles west of Katesh, Tanzania. The woman on the left is wearing a hide cloak, a plant fibre skirt, blue and yellow bead necklaces and silver coil bracelets. The woman on the right is wearing an ornately decorated hide cloak with strings of multicoloured beads. Around her neck is a coiled gold collar, and she is wearing gold and ivory bracelets on her arms and legs.

Two women are sat in a wooden hut surrounded by gourd vessels, in a settlement north west of Mount Hanang, Tanzania. One of the women is sewing strips of hide together to form a cloth. She is wearing a grass skirt, bright blue and yellow necklaces, a gold ornamental earring and a silver coiled armlet. The other woman is wearing gold and ivory bracelets on her arm, gold anklets, and around her neck is a wide coiled gold collar and a variety of multicoloured bead necklaces. Her ear lobe is stretched with a gold ornamental earring.

Portrait of a Christian Datooga woman from Nangwa, near Katesh, Tanzania. She has distinctive scarification marks around her eyes, and is wearing colourful and patterned scarfs around her shoulders and head.

Portrait of a Datooga woman from 20 miles west of Katesh, Tanzania. She is wearing a hide cloak ornately decorated with multicoloured string of beads, around her neck is a gold disc collar and perforated disc pendants handing on hide and bead thongs. Her ear lobes are stretched and pierced with a gold ornament and her face has scarification marks that circle around her eyes.

Knife and sheath. The knife (.1) has a dark wooden handle with a disc at the end. The sheather (.2) is made from brown leather with three sections of reptile skin and a black leather tip. Made by Tama from spring of motor car. Blade cannot be separated from sheath.

Surat el Meiram. Throwing spear with a wooden shaft and metal spearhead. The blade is leaf shaped, with midrib and ridges following the outside edge. The socket has a circular cross section and is decorated at the top with chevrons and grooves. The shaft has a circular cross-section. Used by Sultan Ali Dinar and his relatives.

Tabaga. Spear with a wooden shaft and metal spearhead. The blade is large and leaf shaped, with a midrib, ridges that follow the outside edge and decorated with a few grooves. Split socket, with cloth at the base. The shaft has a circular cross-section.

Dagger or knife with curved iron blade, wooden handle and leather sheath. Khulal or hair pin made from wood. Circular cross-section tapering towards a point; flared at the head with three stacked elements; decorated below the head with black geometric patterns; curved slightly towards the tip.

Numerous carvings, representing human figures. They are strung beneath a canopy of a house made of bamboo sticks, to both sides of a door. The door is framed by carved panels, which show animals (?). The carvings are decorated with painted white and dark pigments. On the left side of the house, a fence is made of several mats. The roof of the house is supported by four pillars, two on each side of the entrance (see also 1998.112.30).

Group of people, some of them sitting and standing on mats, which are spread on the floor. An elderly man, wearing a white turban, is sitting on a stool in the middle, surrounded by sitting and standing male, females and children. The girls and women are wearing scarfs. Sheeps on the right side in the background, two houses behind the group.

European (Frank Christol?), sitting in a room, whose walls are made of mats. The woven mats show a geometric pattern due to different colours. A mask is hanging from the wall. The European sits on a caryatid stool, whose caryatid figures represent human figures. To his left stands a drum and in front of him is a sculpture, showing a seated male figure.

Young man (see 1998.111.30), standing besides a richly carved part of a bed. The carvings show human beings, animals and human heads. The carving rests on some kind of bark (?) or shows the backside of the bed (?).

Three quarter portrait of the Chief of Basoa, sitting in front of a house. He wears a cloth which is decorated with geometric patterns, produced by resist-dyeing, as well as a matching cap. To his left a young boy is standing, holding a fly whisk and a pipe, both decorated with beads. The pipe is made of clay, showing the heas of an elephant. The frame of the entrance is made of carved panels, which show human beings and snakes (?) (see 1998.110.10).

Young child, standing on a caryatid stool. The caryatid figures represent human beings. The stool is flanked by a long rectangular and richly carved panel on each side, standing upright. The one to the left shows four human figures on top of each other, the on the bottom being a female. The figure on the top represents an European, riding on an animal. He wears a white european dress and a pith-helmet. The panel on the right side shows four human figures as well, the first from the bottom thereby placed above an animal (lizard?). On top of this first figure, showing a male, the carver placed two female figures, the right one being significantly smaller than the left one. On top of them there is again a male figure, above which an animal is shown, similar to the ridden animal on top of the left panel. The carvings and the child are placed in front of a house wall, which is made of bamboo sticks. A vertical rectangular segment of the wall is patterend by a geometric design (see also 1998.11.12).

Chief of Banju, sitting on a caryartid stool in front of a house. In the background a group of men is standing, those to his rigth are dressed in  loincloth and wearing caps. Some of the men on the left side are dressed in trousers and long shirts, they are also wearing turbans. The two men to the utmost left are holding lances (see 1998.110.12).
Two thatched mud brick buildings situated on a Bamileke hillside settlement with terraced cultivated fields, near Bamenda.

Chief, sitting in front of a house entrance. He wears a white long shirt, european shoes and a cap. He is flanked by two young men, the one to the left holds a drinking horn, the one to the right holds a pipe. The door is framed by richly carved panels. Mud brick granary in Yasso. The small square structure, which sits atop a base of logs and stones, curves inwards towards a conical thatched roof. Two small human figures have been formed from mud on one of the walls.

A group of Dogon women wearing indigo skirts are lifting water from a well in a village 20 miles west of Koro. Two of the women, one carrying a baby on her back, are using a pulley system to help them lift the water from under ground.
View of a lane with mud and peaked straw roofed huts in a Dogon village 10 km east of Bandiagara.

Portrait of a Dogon woman wearing a variety of beaded necklaces including a Maria Theresa thaler pendant and yellow drop earrings. Around her head she has a silver beaded headband, and her hair is braided with a single braid draped over her forehead. Her lower lip is pierced with a silver ring. She is a holding a large wooden pestle, presumably for grinding grain.

A Dogon woman, carrying a small child on her back, grinding sorghum in a large dug out vessel. More sorghum, waiting to be ground, is kept in a basket next to her. The woman is wearing an indigo skit, and a red, yellow and green bead necklace and white hoop earrings.

This man is definitely not a Luo judging from his personal body adornment. He is probably a Kalenjin as the original record reads 'Lanbua', which can be interpreted as Lumbwa, a term used in colonial days for those Kalenjin (such as Kipsigis or Nandi) who lived around Koru and Kipkelion (formerly Fort Tunnel). It is probable that Evans-Pritchard met this man on the road somewhere, perhaps even in Luo country. [Gilbert Oteyo 9/9/2004]

In the moora Murkito, looking back to the town of Buso. Garite, Hallpike's cook, is on the left, carrying his fly-whisk for him, and the balabat of Buso, the poqalla Olapo Aytya (see 2011.20.1.67) is immediately to his left. The two daka diiruuma commemorate two generation sets who killed enemies in battle. The ceremonial town gateway can be seen to the rear, with the hill Pola in the background.

A group of Luo warriors at Karungu in South Nyanza in full warrior dress with long spears and shields, as well as large headdresses of colobus monkey tail hair and ostrich plumes, posed in a rocky landscape. The adornment and the shields are typical of the late nineteenth and early twentieth century period for the Luo. [Gilbert Oteyo 06/05/05 & CM 27/04/2007]

A group portrait of a seated woman surrounded by young women and younger girls, and described as belonging to Kisumu clan of the Luo, captured in a humorous moment in relaxed fashion despite the posed formality of the group. Their personal adornments are simple glass bead necklaces (tik ng’ut), front aprons (olemo), string waist belt and waist beads (tik nungo) and earrings (stadi). The shaven head hair styles are very youthful and would have been a fashion in the period for young women. [Gilbert Oteyo 06/05/05]

This is the landscape of the area around Kendu Bay in Karachuonyo Location, South Nyanza District. The terrain drops away from the hills above Kendu Bay into the open flat land towards the shore, with Lake Victoria seen in the far background. This is a densely settled area and Luo homesteads can be seen below, often spread out as groups of fenced homesteads with grass thatch huts, surrounded by thick euphorbia fences. [Gilbert Oteyo 9/9/2004]
A car parked on a dirt road, packed with equipment. This is probably the car (registration number B 6895) used to transport Evans-Pritchard on his tour around Luo country in 1936. [CM 29/03/2007]

This is an earthwork of a typical Luo defended homestead enclosure dating to the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. The dug ditch and bank structure is called bur in Luo, and an abandoned home is gunda, which gives the term gunda bur for this type of archaeological earthwork. People lived within the earthwork, where houses were built and cattle tethered, protected by both the earthwork and the surrounding ring ditch. In the original notes, this photo is described as the 'old bur Asembo' and I am inclined to think that this is one of the old earthwork settlements of the Asembo clan of the Luo. Many of these spectacular earthworks still exist in Asembo Location up to day. [Gilbert Oteyo 9/9/2004 & CM 23/03/2007]

An upper body profile portrait of an Acholi man, also photographed by Buchta as an 'Acholi warrior' in another image. He is wearing metal arm and neck rings as well as a leopard skin around his shoulders. His hair is ornamented by stringwork and a plume at the back of his head, and his skull shape suggests possible deformation. The image seems to have been taken sometime in January 1879 when Buchta travelled through Acholi country en route to Bunyoro.

Lui Junior Secondary School written in English and Arabic outside the school compound. Two huts and a building can be seen in the distance. The school was built in 1975 by the Sudan Council of Churches. The first school was opened in Lui by Dr, Frazer, a missionary, who brought Christianity to the area in the 1920's, built a church, a school and a hospital in the area, and brought peace as well. Between 1965-72, during the civil war, the Moru Misa people scattered into the hills, and were only just settling back again when we visited. Some still hadn't returned. Patti Langton [28/07/2009]

Decoratively carved grave marker by a roadside. This is one of a number of old wooden grave markers along the road from Mundri to Amadi.  A village can be seen behind. The road-builders moved the road specially to avoid them. Co-worker Andrea told us that these grave markers were used before the current style of  graves as seen in informant Deborah's compound. Deborah's account of them was that grave markers were used when there was no body, if the family member had died far away - to bring the 'soul' home. This grave marker has three 'rings' carved at the top. There used to be specialist craftsmen who made the grave markers. (See also 2008.78.1.41). One of the expedition landrovers can be seen in the background. Patti Langton [23/11/2010]

In this image informant Deborah stands to the side of her father's grave, which is a mixture of Christian and traditional, with the tall vertical megalith on a Christian-style base. He was a chief. Patti Langton [23/03/2009]

A young girl sits on a mat, in front of the entrance to her hut making pottery coils, BIRI BIRI. In front of her is the beginning of a pot, about five coils are already built up on top of an old pottery base, KAGYE,  which is used to create the shape. The girl is adding a coil to the pot. She keeps it moist with water in a metal pot beside her. There is a sequence of this pot being made, unfortunately I've not quite filed it in the right order, but you can see where it goes wrong by the number of coils! The long stick beside her is her walking stick, she had polio as a young child.  (See 2008.78.2.90-101; also 2008.78.1.12). Patti Langton [30/03/2009]
A Moru grave, one of a cluster. It is round, with a flat slab on top. This will have been an elder's grave. Patti Langton [11/05/2009]

A friend of informant Deborah, Naomi Tudrinwa, is making a pot. She sits on a mat, with a metal bowl of water beside her to keep the pot moist. She is using roulettes, probably a LAGIRI, a palm fibre roller.  A young girl sits watching beside her.  (See 2008.78.2.145-151). In later photos we see her firing her pots. 2008.78.1.16 shows this.  Patti Langton [19/05/2009]

Women stay in a special birthing hut to have their babies. Deborah, the main informant,  constructed this hut for her daughter. The hut entrance faces north. After the birth a shelter of grasses is put round the hut. If the baby is a girl mother and baby stay for 4 days afterwards, 3 days if it is a boy. Traditionally the boy would be wrapped in special bark cloth. Today all babies are wrapped in cotton. [Patti Langton 02/03/2009]

A set of old stone axe-heads and other stone tools, laid out on the ground by Surur the rain-maker for Evans-Pritchard to photograph them (although not touch them) from their home along with his hair clippings in a pot beneath the eaves of his stake-walled hut. These stones were called landa loma - stones of Loma, a spiritual connection with rain-making. During rain-making Surur would place these stones along with magical medicines in a pot with rock-pool water and sprinkle to the east where the next day was to arrive from [light leakage on negative?].

Two carvings, one with horn-shaped elongations, tallying the numbers of large animals killed by the person buried beneath, or sometimes the kills of a relative. Graves were commonly grouped together near a settlement (visible in the background). These carvings were understood as a means of honouring the dead but did not have any particular ritual meaning.

A monoxylous side-blown instrument leaning against a tree with end ornamented with two notches possibly representing a human head. The Bongo were noted by early travellers both for their wood-working crafts as well as variety of musical instruments and occasions.

A long wooden rain-post (riyak) with maize heads and medicines attached, stuck into the ground under a large nilotic shea-butter tree, Vitellaria paradoxa ssp. nilotica, a slow-growing hardwood fruit tree indigenous to northern Uganda and Southern Sudan. During drought this post was the focus for rain-making rituals involving the sprinkling of durra (Sorghum bicolor) over an assembled crowd by a rain-maker (biriak).

A stone mound erected over a man's grave (dodo) surmounted by a short pointed stake with a decorated gourd attached to it. Around the mound are six carved posts tallying different large animals killed by the deceased, one of which (to the right) is also surmounted by a carved likeness of the man. These carved figures were considered representations of the deceased, put up to honour the individual, but not serving any ritual purpose [cloudy image].

A stone mound near a hut erected over a man's grave (dodo) with three carved posts surmounting the top tallying twenty elephants killed in the hunt by the deceased, placed as a means of honouring him. Around the mound are five more carved posts (some with arrows stuck in them). Three are visible in this image: the tip of a carved post in the likeness of the deceased with a tally of two hippo killed, then to the right a forked post tallying six rhino and lastly in the foreground a forked post tallying five buffalo, with a ?bowl and ?piece of matting stuck on it.

View of a large stone carving at the ancient Maya site of Quirigua located near the banks of the Motagua river in the department of Izabal, Guatemala. The photograph shows a man standing beside the south face of a carved stone zoomorph known by archaeologists as Zoomorph B, as it was first described by Alfred Maudslay in his seminal publication of the Quirigua site in his multi-volume Archaeology (1889–1902): 'This monument is lying on three large slabs of stone, which are well shown in Plates IX and X [ie. this photograph]. It is carved into the shape of a great dragon, with a human head, bust, and hands issuing from the dragon's mouth. In Plate XII, a, the two great eyes of the dragon, with hanging eyelashes and crossed bands over the eyeballs, can be clearly seen. The upper jaw is raised so that the row of incisor teeth shows above the grotesque mask which surmounts the human head.' More recent scholarship dates the zoomorph (also known as Monument 2) to 9.17.10.0.0, 12 Ahau 8 Pax (Maya calendar), or A.D. 780 in the standard Western (Gregorian) calendar. Identified over the years variously as a tiger, dragon, turtle and toad, the carving is now understood by scholars to represent a supernatural crocodilian, sometimes termed the Cosmic Monster. The monument was created during the later part of the sixty-year reign of K'ak' Tiliw Chan Yopaat and marked the close of an era in the Maya calendar.  It was one of a number of stelae and zoomorphs erected at Quirigua as part of a complex building programme which took place at the height of the city-state's power during the Late Classic period, and whose primary aim was to legitimate and reinforce the power of the ruler.

View of a large stone carving at the ancient Maya site of Quirigua located near the banks of the Motagua river in the department of Izabal, Guatemala. The photograph shows the south face and east side of a carved stone zoomorph known by archaeologists as Zoomorph P, as it was first described by Alfred Maudslay in his seminal publication of the Quirigua site in his multi-volume Archaeology (1889–1902): 'This great monument, which must weigh nearly twenty tons, stands, like the other monolithic animals, on a foundation of three large flat stones, which are not visible in the photographs. When first found it presented a most enigmatic appearance, for it was not until the earth had been dug away around the base that the great hands or flippers could be seen, which proved the main design to be the representation of a great turtle. The head of the animal, which faces nearly south, is surrounded by a hieroglyphic inscription.' More recent scholarship dates the zoomorph (also known as Monument 16) to 9.18.5.0.0, 4 Ahau 13 Ceh (Maya calendar), or A.D. 795 in the standard Western (Gregorian) calendar. Identified over the years as various different animals, the carving is now understood by scholars to represent a Cosmic Monster with a mountain on its back. The monument was created during the reign of Sky Xul and marked the close of an era in the Maya calendar. It was one of a number of stelae and zoomorphs erected at Quirigua as part of a complex building programme which took place during the Late Classic period, and whose primary aim was to legitimate and reinforce the power of the ruler.

View of a large stone carving at the ancient Maya site of Quirigua located near the banks of the Motagua river in the department of Izabal, Guatemala. The photograph shows the south face of a carved stone stela known by archaeologists as Stela A, as it was first described by Alfred Maudslay in his seminal publication of the Quirigua site in his multi-volume Archaeology (1889–1902): 'This monument faces south and stands in line with the stelae C and D in front of the mound which forms the northern boundary of the Great Plaza. Owing to the decayed condition of the stone, the design on the pedestal which supports the figure is somewhat obscure both on the front and on the back of the monument; but in each case parts of the profile of a grotesque mask can be traced.' More recent scholarship dates the stela (also known as Monument 1) to 9.17.5.0.0 (Maya calendar), or A.D. 775 in the standard Western (Gregorian) calendar. The monument was created during the later part of the sixty-year reign of K'ak' Tiliw Chan Yopaat and marked the close of an era in the Maya calendar. It was one of a number of stelae and zoomorphs erected at Quirigua as part of a complex building programme which took place at the height of the city-state's power during the Late Classic period, and whose primary aim was to legitimate and reinforce the power of the ruler.

View of buildings at Pescado pueblo, a Zuni 'summer resort', in a considerable state of disrepair.  According to James Stevenson's original note for this photograph (prepared circa 1885), 'Pescado appears to be in a partial state of ruin due to negligence and irregular occupancy by the Indians.'

Portrait of a Zuni woman, standing, carrying a large decorated pottery vessel on her head.  According to James Stevenson's original note for this photograph (prepared circa 1885), the photograph depicts 'a Zuni squaw, holding a water-vase on the top of the head, just as they appear while carrying water from the well to the house.  This is a fair specimen of the Zuni woman as she appears in her daily tasks.  The bulky, clumsy leggings form part of the moccasins.  A long buck-skin strip about four inches wide which is attached to the moccasin is wrapped around the leg nearly to the knee, each layer slightly over-lapping the other, the end being tightly inserted beneath the last layer of buckskin to hold it in place.  The gown is woven from native yarn dyed black or dark blue with a vegetable dye.  The garment is first made as a blanket, nearly square; the ends are then sewed together, one side being left open.  This open end forms the bottom of the dress, while apertures are made in the other for the head and arms.  One shoulder is left partly exposed while the other is beneath the dress.'

No inner moss bag. Back of cradleboard is plain, painted green.  The bar going across the back of the board, which ends in red painted disks, has been moved upwards. Hair brush of rye grass roots with handle sewed in buckskin
Portrait of Hin-han Du-ta; Mdewakanton Sioux
Food or mush bowl made by Old Ell Design, from the collection of C. Hartman. Coiled, bundle foundation, spiral start.
Food or mush bowl with red wool and quail feathers, from unknown collection. Coiled, bundle foundation, non-interlocking stitches, clockspring start.
Man's comb-wood edged with brass; decorated on one side with 6 small metal discs
Man's cotton vest. Plain weave, paired warps & wefts. Sleeveless. Brass buttons.
Cotton hammock made of twisted cord. Each end comes together in a bundle with cord wrapped around it; 17 tassels on one side where the cord has been sewn across perpendicularly.
Wooden spindle. Whorl is a flat disc of wood or possible seed. The spindle shaft is thickened in the centre.
Single-sided, rectangular body stamp made of wood; design of vertical lines.
Manioc sieve. Circular with frame made of bundled fibres, woven with a central diamond design.

Tawahemen. Woven black and white basket with circular rim and square base. Cane around rim, attached with fibre string. Ankatapuhpe (traditional Panare) design with modern Panare weave pattern (one over three).
Kerosene lamp, made from a repurposed old tin can. The can is white and has 'Liga para Frenos' written on it. The fibre wick protrudes from the top through a hole in the can's red metal screw cap.

Mankowaye. Curare pot. Wrapped in leaves and tied with thread. Presumed to contain curare, a broad term for various alkaloid arrow poisons produced from plant extracts. Used as a paralysing agent in hunting

Watta. Blowpipe or blow gun made from two long lengths of cane, the narrowest one sliding inside the largest one. Flared mouthpiece secured to the pipe with resin or gum. At the end of the blowpipe is a stopper of resign or gum preventing the wider cane tube from sliding out.
Human figure made of walrus ivory, dressed in white fur with a radiating hairstyle created from human hair and facial ornaments of bird quill.

Changina. A large, cylindrical basket with a flat oval base made with tamshi using a hexagonal weave. One length of cane forms the edge and is enclosed by strips. A bark strap supports the bottom of the basket and is then tied around the rim and extends, allowing it to be carried around the forehead. Used by both sexes it is the largest basket for carrying yucca.
Medicine used against snake bites, grated into water and taken orally. Eight seeds in half shells.

Bag - Quadrangular string bag of fibre, with a design of six fields each consisting of four black stripes. Attached to the top are 16 cane loops which form the drawstring mechanism and from where the plant fibre string runs down to the right and left bottom corners of the bag. The string loops on either side and is worn over the shoulders, with the bag worn on the back.

Vayavay; kun. Woman’s skirt of yellow cotton cloth partly open at one side, and fastened with a loop and strap at the waist. Panel of black velvet appliquéd to lower edge and decorated with butterflies, snakes and anthropomorphic faces, wearing ovoid linear headdresses, in orange, green, yellow, white and blue glass beads, intersected by sequins. Row of aluminium discs stitched along top edge of panel; band of repeated short linear beads along bottom edge of panel, which is further strung with metal bells on small beaded loops.

Bhut. A pair of trousers made by Sherbegum and Gul Sahar. They are made of black synthetic cotton fabric with a wide waist band and narrow ankles. The ankles are embroidered with yellow and green wool in ziz-zag patterns and trimmed with loops of black, green and yellow wool.

Kupas. Shell headdress made by Sherbegum. Made from a piece of woven woollen black, red and blue striped fabric, with a red woollen pompom on the top, and heavily embellished with cowry shells, coloured beads, white buttons, small metal bells and metal discs and band of coloured woven fabric with tassels. Part of a Kalasha costume.
Bow; Arrow - A: self-bow of bamboo, with twisted fibre string. B: long, reed arrow, with tanged, iron head. No feather
Round basket, used for holding women's decorations
Charm - " Lower jaw of deer" . Obviously the lower jaw of a pig though. Regarded as sacred

Syaanmo. Shirt and skirt worn only by Khhlyeprin shaman. Must be made all in one day, before the sun goes down. These costumes used to be made by the shaman's mother, but now are now made by a tailor and modelled after the old example.

Thuhnga. Iridescent conical shell used as a horn. Always blown at the beginning of the ritual before playing the drum. There are two types of blowing, one for god and one for evil spirits (to scare them).

Saamon. A wand made out of a bunch of peacock feathers bound with twigs at the bottom. Used by Pa-chyu shaman during ritual. When not being held during ritual, they are stood in a bowl of millet (you cannot put them on the ground). The peacock is noted for being very beautiful and powerful. A peacock feather can be used in various ways, e.g. if worried that insects will eat a book, a bit of the feather is put with the book.
Ornament - Head ornament, comprising woven band, from which hangs a fringe of coloured beads and seeds

Manchu woman's robe of heavy, blue woven cotton. Half length sleeves folded over with yellow lining and trim. Upright collar and round neck, with knot and loop fastening at one side; and a short panel underneath with dye in floral shape in corner. The garment widens from the waist and has large side slits; the front and back are decorated with an embroidered border of flowers, birds and fish using pink, orange, blue and cream thread; and an appliqué ribbon of floral design in green, blue, purple and pink above in geometric shape. This is also present around the neck and upper fastening, with floral pale yellow embroidering on the sleeves.

Silver nose ring with coral and glass beads. Loop of thick wire, flattened at one end and decorated with two circular metal and bead elements; smaller circular element decorated with granulated projections and with a blue bead at the centre; larger circular element decorated with granulated projections, three blue glass beads and four coral beads on thin wire.

A long coat [A] with waistcoat [B]. The front of the coat is made from purple silk with multicoloured floral brocade, with a trim of black velvet; the waist has striped band of black, red and gold; the sleeves are made from green silk brocade with purple patterned cuffs, and there appears to be wool wadding in the layers of the sleeves. The back of the coat is made from plain blue silk and cotton. The waistcoat is made of dark blue brocade silk, with a trim of red and gold, and is tied at the neck by strands of red and gold.

Black turban of crepe silk, worn by a married woman. Rectangular strip of black crepe silk, gathered in three places with blue stitching; one end folded back on itself; two lengths of cream paper with traces of red and blue dye are stitched together and attached to part of the turban.
Aude. Ceremonial iron arrow. It is over-sized and leaf-shaped, with a central ridge, and is tanged at one end. There are nicks along the edges.
Portrait sculpture in plaster of Budi, a Saora girl.
Beaten ?brass headband, with raised hammer decoration. Non-ceremonial and worn by ordinary tribesmen.

Oplecko. Woman's shirt. White with embroidered decorations in pink, purple, green, orange, blue, and white around the cuffs, shoulders, and neckline. The sleeves are gathered and end in lace panels. There are ties at the front.

Man's shirt. White with embroidered floral decorations around the neckline, collar, shoulders, and cuffs. There are buttons on the sleeves made of metal covered with thread. There are ties at the neck.
Red shawl with floral print. The shawl is bordered by a red ribbon and has wool tassels.
Beige table cloth with lace trimming. The lace is white with a beige diamond pattern.
Sheath; knife - Antler-handled knife (A) in antler sheath (B) with leather thong.

Cylindrical blown glass lantern with tin fittings and conical tin cover decorated with perforated curvilinear ornament. Loop for suspension at top. Tin candle holder secured to base. Two pieces of broken glass are inside.

Tamata. Votive offering. Representation of a young child in brown wax. A loop of string protrudes from the top of its head, suggesting a point of suspension. The head has a large indentation on its left side, possibly representing a deformity. There is a patch of white powder on the back of the head on its right side.

Tamata. Votive offering of an arm, modelled in green wax. The hand is represented by a square slab of wax with lines showing the divisions between the fingers, the thumb is separate. The arm is slightly bent at the elbow and a loop of string threaded through a hole in the upper arm suggests a point of suspension.

Hanging religious charm, highly decorated with plastic, multi-coloured (predominately green and yellow) beads and sequins. Central metal disc with colour printed pictures on both sides. The Madonna & Child and St. Nicholas. Each picture is surrounded by a row of sequins secured by small beads and metal pins. The edge of the central disc has radiating, cylindrical beads tipped with small, round beads and sequins. At the top and bottom of the central disc are rosettes of circular, flat beads and there are large, round beads on the outer edges. Attached to the top is a gold coloured, metal chain, providing a means of suspension. A gold coloured, plastic cross hangs from the bottom, flanked by two translucent strawberries.
Batik textile by Yipati Kuyata typical of that produced by textile artists in the Ernabella community.

Bilum bag netted from thick twine in double figure of 8 rows. Reddish brown loop stitching attaches separately netted rim band. Netted carrying strap crosses over from top corners. Design of contrasting blue and reddish brown dyed twine netted in against natural pale brown colour. Three broad horizontal bands each composed of paired blue and reddish brown narrow bands, and with natural bands left between each broad band. Each with a slightly darker brown stripe through their centres. Made by Tshuosh, in neighbourhood of Berui village. Original accession notes: " Pattern worked in dyed string. Carried suspended from the head by women. Bought from Tshuosh by Iatmul." Good.
Four sago-beetle heads are carved in profile round a lozenge shaped piece of wood which has a narrow double-rimmed hole piercing its centre vertically.

Pair of false breasts worn by men of fine twined cane work cones with tubular apexes, one apex broken off, the other extending to a slightly expanded nozzle. Coated with thick black pigment. Paint peeling off, rims frayed.

Flat-backed ovoid head with strongly pointed protruding forehead. Hole pierces top of head. No ears. Narrow raised slanting eyes, raised ovoid mouth. Light wood with black/brown colouring overall. Rounded chin, tassel loop through pierced nostrils.
Large turbo shell whorl with iridescent inside and outer surface painted with design of wavy red lines alternating with white. Semi-circular wickerwork pouch, with edges sewn together, attached.

Ornament - Roughly ovoid shell cusp with natural striations on outside and smooth polished inside. Irregular lip ridge at top. Pierced by two small circular holes on one long side, through which a rough knotted length of twine is fastened. Twine broken, outer surface badly stained. Original accession notes: " Ornament for breast or head made of portion of melon shell and worn by either sex. For use of this ornament see Handbook, Photographs -. In these photographs a dish of European origin has been substituted for WOKTAI. Masks nos. 1935.54 and 1935.167 are decorated with representations of WOKTAI in basketwork and wood respectively." Poor

Arrow with bamboo point with nicked sides at base, rounded foreshaft tip showing. Point binding of twisted cord, 3 diagonal crossings over plain coiling. Wooden foreshaft, uncoloured, waisted in 3 places. 3 rings project at each of the upper 2 waists, 2 & 2 rings incised on upper expansion. Shaft binding of diagonally crossed cane strings, stained red. Tapering bamboo shaft with remains of red stain.

A ceramic pot of red brown fabric, with an everted decorated in small grooves, convex top half, raised ridge around the middle, and rounded bottom half with a flat base. Two handles attached from the neck to mid section; one possibly incorporating a spout which is now blocked. Decorated with grooves and patterns in dark red slip.

Bracelet consisting of two parallel strings of cylindrical coconut beads interspersed with rectangular white beads spanning the two strings (possibly armadillo shell). The bracelet is secured by tying the string.
A necklace made of polished seeds; spherical black interspersed with 22 biconical red Abrus precatorius seeds. The brown seeds have a vertically ridged surface; some are abraded.

Pot of pink ware with pronounced everted rim, rounded body and flat, wide base. Decorated with undulating pattern filled with small line marks. Black firing marks present across body and base. Sections missing from rim.

Small burnished pot with a flat base, globular body and long narrow neck. The rim is upright and the pot is decorated with two incised horizontal lines at the base of the neck. Pot contains a fluffy substance, possibly loose wool or cotton.

Pot of red ware. Everted rim and narrow mouth, shouldered body and flat base. Decorated below neck with linear patterns incised with a stick. Horizontal band at neck followed by irregular triangular patterns extending over the shoulder. Burnished at neck. Firing marks at base.

Woven cotton cloth, rectangular in shape, white background, stripes of orange and red running down long edges, short ends with two black lines and short dotted lines meeting them perpendicularly, closer to the centre are lines of red and orange with zigzags and geometric patterns in blue.

Pencil drawing - 1 unaccessioned portrait in pencil on paper of a Toda woman in profile. It is inscribed in pencil 'Sinraj / 16 years / mantle of hair' on the front and the back of the mount it is inscribed 'Toda / Mrs Milward' in pencil.

A green silk skirt lined with a red cotton and a red cotton waist band with tie. The green silk is embellished with metal sequins with clear glass beads above a row of mirrors set in gold repoussé frames and a band of woven metal thread. At the bottom there is a wide band of orange cotton with red and green velvet appliqué, mirrors in gold frames and metal sequins with clear glass beads. There is a stiff canvas sewn in between the bottom band and the lining.
A necklace consisting of small faceted gold gilt beads, pointed beads with small round projections, and small wooden beads towards the ends; they are strung onto a length of plant fibre.

Earring or pendant made from gilded brass. A pair of dangling ornaments connected by a length of wire; both ornaments are composed of three metal discs hanging below one another with a fringe of rectangular pendants around the edge of each.

Red velvet cap [.1] with embellishments and veil, and a velvet strap for attachment [.2]. Domed cap of dark red velvet lined with red cotton and with a stuffed conical form on top; top is decorated with white cotton diamonds, black velvet, gold trim, silver glass beads, and silver sequins and spiralled wire; bottom of cap has a silver metallic trim with silver glass beads; at the crown is a tassel of crimped metal wire and a veil of netted and starched cotton with a rectangular border of gold trim, sequins and glass beads supported on a strip of canvas.

Woman's waist cloth, rectangular in shape comprised of two pieces of woven cotton sewn together, white background, long outside edges with thick red bands, thin stripes of red running lengthways intersected on one end with thicker bands of red running across short edge.
Necklace comprising strings of blue, yellow and white beads on red thread. Worn by young men and women.
Imitation coin necklace worn by young men and women.
Nose ornament. Worn by women on one side of the nose.
Axe  - Two axes with straight wooden handles bound with brass wire. A) long convex blade, T-shaped. B) long concave blade, T-shaped.

Arrow  - Six arrows. A-B) each with flat, iron head, shouldered (female arrow), with triple, straight feathering (from vultures). Known as " villa ambu" . C) with spike iron head (male arrow), with quadruple, spiral feathering (from peacock). Known as " guka" . D) with wooden point and straight, triple feathering. Known as " ramalu ambu" .
Straight, bamboo digging stick with iron ferrule and spike.
Simple bow made from wood; circular cross-section, tapered towards each end; strip of leather around one end; wide band of leather, possibly grip, near centre of bow.

Bamboo quiver (.1) covered in leather with a stitched leather lid attached by a long narrow hide shoulder strap. Poisoned arrows (.2-16) have long narrow cane shafts with feather fletchings, eight of which have lost their feathers but the cotton binding remains. 11 of the arrows have metal leaf shaped heads, two have traditional arrow shaped heads and two have long metal spikes.

A waist ornament made from five long strands of metal, black, white, red and translucent beads, strung in an alternating colour pattern with metal strips in between. Strand of string on the two ends, possibly for fastening.

Kameushu. A long man’s shirt made from cotton with a white, grey and blue check pattern, with zig-zag details. The shirt has long sleeves, a short collar, waist band, and a full pleated skirt section. The shirt is fastened down the front with four shell buttons, and there is pleating either side of the buttons; the cuffs are also fastened with shell buttons.

A pair of red leather shoes with upturned toes with large brown wool pom-poms attached. There is a stripe of brown, cream, blue and red threads down the centre of the shoes; the leather has been stitched together with cream and black threads.
A cream cotton hat with a flat round top and flaring sides. Decorated with gold silk embroidery in bands of patterns around the sides and a star shape on the top.
Lapudzi. Pair of woollen socks knitted with a ribbed cuff in stripes of navy, blue, pink, green, maroon and white. Tied together.
A pair of navy blue wool leggings, with a brown cotton braid trim. They have a tab with a navy blue cord attached at the top, and metal hook and eye fastenings at the ankles.

Beaded necklace, comprising a long, white textile tube decorated with red, blue and white glass beads arranged in a zigzag pattern. One end has a loop in red, white and blue, the other end has a bulbous yellow ornament with loops of yellow and blue beads. Loops of blue beads are attached at three points along the tube.
Spear, with small, leaf-shaped, socketed iron blade with central midrib. Long shaft tapers towards the end. The surface of the shaft is slightly uneven due to the natural grain of the wood.
Spear, with small, leaf-shaped, socketed iron blade with central midrib. Long shaft tapers towards the end. The surface of the shaft is slightly uneven due to the natural grain of the wood.
Spearhead from a throwing spear. The blade is leaf shaped with a prominent midrib. The socket is long and split, with a circular cross-section. Shaft is 1922.1253.2.
Wooden shaft of a throwing spear; the spearhead end tapers to a point. The shaft has a circular cross-section with natural knots present. Spearhead is 1922.1253.1.

A pipe, with a burnished black pottery bowl [.1] and a wooden stem [.2]. The bowl is cylindrical with a rounded base, and is decorated with triangular bands of incised cross-hatching. It has a cylindrical stem, also decorated with incised cross-hatching, and five incised rings near the socket where the wooden part of the stem meets the ceramic part. The rim is chipped, and the bowl has been reconstructed.

Wooden spoon carved from a single piece of wood. Bowl is roughly oval, with one tapered end. Back of the bowl is flat, extending to a slightly curved handle, almost at a right angle to the bowl. Rim of the bowl has burnt decoration.

Knife with sheath. Bunyoro chief's knife. The knife (.1) has a long iron blade with two incised lines along the middle and a small oval cut-out section near the handle. Wooden handle with carved decoration and a protruding disc at the end. The sheath (.2) is wooden, highly decorated on one side with a protruding loop, possibly for suspension. The sheath is broken into two.

Spear. Leaf-shaped brass socketed head and tapering ferrule with long wooden shaft, circular in cross-section. Replica of royal spear placed at the head of the graves of deceased Kabakas in the mausoleum known as Mutesa's tomb at Kasubi, near Mengo.
Woven flared ring-stand for a vessel. Decorated with a spiral of red and black fibres.
